abstract: Functional traits can influence a plant's ability to establish and spread in a new environment. Examining traits associated with resource acquisition and defense may help explain why some introduced species become invasive while others do not. This study aimed to determine whether invasive and non-invasive Lonicera species differed in growth-related, physical-defense, and chemical-defense traits at the Arnold Arboretum of Harvard University in Boston, Massachusetts. Invasive species were predicted to exhibit traits associated with greater resource acquisition while maintaining distinct, but not necessarily reduced, chemical defenses. To investigate these differences, 12 traits were assessed across six invasive and eight non-invasive species, with the non-invasive group comprising three native and five non-invasive exotic species. Overall, trait composition differed between invasive and non-invasive species. Invasive species exhibited higher specific leaf area and lower leaf thickness, suggesting that invasiveness among the sampled species was associated with differences in leaf resource acquisition and structure, rather than a consistent reduction in chemical defense. Future research should include additional individuals and populations to determine whether these patterns occur more broadly and can help predict plant invasiveness.
